deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. Together with the previous page (classes I–V of lattice points, signs ε = ±1 fixed by the sign of the imaginary part of im/(p−p°), 'Specialregeln' with 2bη = a − 2x + aω, …) and the next page (a worked example with m = 3−2i of norm 13, M = −1−6i of norm 37, μ = 9+20i, (1+i)M + (−2+i)m = 1, mM = −15−16i), this page belongs to Gauss's unpublished work on the biquadratic character of one Gaussian prime with respect to another. He counts Gaussian lattice points in a region cut out by m and M, with signs, to obtain a 'Decident' (the decisive quantity). Its residue (mod 4) fixes the power of i that is the biquadratic residue symbol. This is a Gauss-lemma / lattice-point approach, analogous to his third and fifth proofs of quadratic reciprocity, applied to Z[i].

(1) Heading: 'The first method now gives the following result.' The heading carries a struck-out archival number 43d/10, and the folio is numbered (22).

4·Decident =
  I:   Σε over all class-I points − 4Σε over those with y an integer and [x] even;
  II:  −(Σε over all class-II points) + 4Σε over those with [x] even and [y] odd;
  IV:  +4Σε over those points where [x] and [y] are not both even;
  + Q.
Here [x] denotes the integer part (floor) of x. Class III gets no explicit term. Either it drops out or it is absorbed elsewhere; this is unclear from the page alone. The page gives no derivation of this identity. It is stated as the outcome of the 'first method' and is checked numerically on the next page: Decident = −2, Q = −5, 'Gut'.

(2) Boundary correction Q, by the signs of A and B. These are evidently the real and imaginary parts, or associated sign data, of one of the numbers (the details are unclear):
- A+, B+: Q = −Int(μωi) ± Int(½m − μω)
- A+, B−: Q = −Int(μω) ± Int(½mi − μωi)
- A−, B−: Q = −Int(−μωi) ± Int(½m + μω)
- A−, B+: Q = −Int(−μω) ± Int(½mi + μωi)
The cases are related by multiplying the argument by successive powers of i (rotation by a unit). The note on the sign was first 'upper sign for M−1 divisible by 4', then changed to 'not divisible', and the whole sentence was struck out. 'Int.' / 'Intens.' must be some integer-part or lattice-count functional of a Gaussian number; its exact definition is not on this page.

(3) 'The following table shows this.' A first attempt, a table keyed by whether ¼(M−1) and ¼(γ−1) are whole numbers or fractions (Ganz/Bruch), is struck out. It is replaced by a numerical table:
- Rows: the sign pairs of (a, b), namely ++, +−, −−, −+.
- Column groups: the four sign pairs of (A, B).
- Each group has two sub-columns, apparently 'm impar' and 'm par' (labelled 'impar' and 'm impar' under the first group).
- Entries are small integers: +2, 0, −3, +1, … down to −6.

(4) Interpolation by sign polynomials. Gauss writes 2Q as a multilinear polynomial in the sign variables A, B, α, b ∈ {±1}:
- 'Pars prior ipsius 2Q' = −3 − αb + Aα + Ab + Bα − Bb.
- Whole 2Q, m odd ('für m impar' was struck through, but the sense remains):
  2Q = −3 + 4A − B − b + αA + αB + bA − bB − αbAB.
- m even ('m par'):
  2Q = −3 + 2A + B − ½α + b + ½αA + ½αB + bA − bB − ½αAB + 2bAB − αbAB.

Observation (mine): the four half-integer terms combine as −½α(1−A)(1−B). This product is 0 or −2α when A, B = ±1, so the expression is an integer only if the variables are ±1 signs, not 0/1 indicators. This confirms the reading of the variables as signs. Both formulas give even values on {±1}^4, consistent with their being 2Q. This is the standard device of writing a function on {±1}^n as a polynomial (Fourier–Walsh expansion), which Gauss also uses for the supplementary laws.
errors: The rule fixing which sign (upper or lower) in Q applies was first tied to 4 | M−1, then changed to 'untheilbar', then cancelled. The page leaves this sign rule unresolved.
A first version of the Ganz/Bruch table is abandoned (struck out).

I could not reproduce the table entries from the printed odd-m polynomial under the obvious identification (α, b = signs of a, b; table entry = 2Q). For A = B = + it gives 2α − b − αb, i.e. 0, 4, −2, −2 for (α,b) = ++, +−, −−, −+, whereas the first sub-column reads +2, 0, −3, +1. Most likely the variables or columns mean something else (e.g. different parameters, or values taken mod 8). Any agreement cannot be confirmed from the page alone.
Class III does not appear in the expression for 4·Decident. This is not necessarily an error, but it is unexplained.
The 4·Decident identity is asserted without proof; its only support is the numerical check on the next page.

results.what: Expression of 4×(the decisive quantity for the biquadratic character) as signed counts Σε over classes of lattice points with parity conditions on floors, plus a boundary term Q
results.modern_name: Gauss-lemma / lattice-point (Eisenstein-type) approach to the biquadratic residue symbol and biquadratic reciprocity in Z[i]
results.usually_credited_to: Biquadratic reciprocity: first published proofs by Eisenstein (1844), Jacobi in his 1836–37 lectures; Gauss-lemma analogues later by Eisenstein, Busche and others

results.what: Case table for the boundary correction Q by quadrant (signs of A, B), the cases related by multiplication by powers of i
results.modern_name: Unit/quadrant normalization of boundary terms in Z[i] lattice-point counts
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Nachlass on biquadratic residues); standard technique

results.what: Writing 2Q as a multilinear polynomial in ±1 sign variables A, B, α, b (separately for m odd and m even)
results.modern_name: Multilinear (Walsh/Fourier) interpolation of a function on {±1}^n; character-style formulas like those of the supplementary laws
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss's own style, as in the supplementary laws of Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum II

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss is known to have possessed, but never published, a proof of biquadratic reciprocity. Nachlass fragments and later reconstructions (e.g. discussed by Lemmermeyer) indicate a lattice-point / Gauss-lemma approach in Z[i]. This page is a working detail of such a computation, with case-wise correction terms and sign-polynomial interpolation. It adds concrete evidence of an elaborated counting method but no new theorem beyond what is attributed to him.
